title: Capstone: Clubs and Leagues
summary: Build a whole app, start to finish: plan the data, build an ASP.NET Core API with Entity Framework Core, and a React frontend that talks to it. Explorers build the Grove Club Hub; Builders build the Junior League app.
objectives: Plan an app's data as tables, and test it with SQL
Build an API that reads and writes that data with ASP.NET Core and Entity Framework Core
Build a React frontend that fetches from your own API and shows the results
Handle what can go wrong between the two: errors, validation and loading
Finish and share a full-stack project of your own

lessons.title: Show your clubs on the page
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Your app, both halves

The **Grove Club Hub** has a server: a C# **API** (*Application Programming Interface*) that knows every club in the Grove. It also has a React page. Right now the page is empty, because nobody told it to ask the server anything.

Today you join the two halves. That makes you a **full-stack** developer: you build the page *and* the server it talks to.

```
Page (React)  --- fetch("/api/clubs") --->  Server (C#)
Page (React)  <------- the clubs, as JSON ---  Server (C#)
```

### Asking your own server

You've used `fetch` before, with the practice API. To ask *your* server, start the address with a slash and leave out the website:

```jsx
fetch("/api/clubs")
```

A path that starts with `/` means "the server this page came from". Your server runs right next to the page, so that's your C# API.

### C# names and JSON names

In C#, the club's properties are `Name` and `Meets`. When the server turns a club into **JSON** (*JavaScript Object Notation*), it starts each name with a small letter:

```json
{ "id": 1, "name": "Acorn Artists", "meets": "Friday" }
```

So in React you write `club.name` and `club.meets`. Write `club.Name` and you get nothing at all!

### Ask once

Put the `fetch` inside `useEffect`, with `[]` at the end. The `[]` means "only when the page opens", so the page asks one time.

### The Network tab

Next to **Preview** there's a **Network** tab. It lists every request your page sends to your server, and what came back. If your list stays empty, look there first.

### New words

- **Full-stack**: building both halves of an app, the page people see and the server behind it.
- **API** (*Application Programming Interface*): the server's list of things you can ask it, like `GET /api/clubs`.
- **JSON** (*JavaScript Object Notation*): the text format the server uses to send data to the page.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A snack list that gets its snacks from its own C# server. Open the **Network** tab to see the page ask `GET /api/snacks`. Then try adding `"Dandelions"` to the list in `api/Program.cs` and press **▶ Run**.

lessons.title: The standings page
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Connecting the frontend to your API

Every web app you use is two programs. The **frontend** runs in the browser; the **backend** runs on a server and owns the data. The work in between is the same in almost every job: the frontend sends HTTP requests, reads JSON, and shows something sensible whether the answer is good, bad or slow. In this milestone the Junior League's React page starts talking to the ASP.NET Core API you know from the Web API course.

### Same-origin requests

```jsx
fetch("/api/standings?division=north")
```

A path with no scheme or host goes to the page's own **origin** (scheme, host and port). In Codegrove your API answers those requests right next to the page. In a real project the React dev server (Vite, on port 5173) and the API (on port 5080) are different origins, so you add a **proxy** to the dev server that forwards `/api`:

```js
// vite.config.js
export default {
  server: {
    proxy: { "/api": "http://localhost:5080" },
  },
};
```

The browser only ever talks to 5173, so the code above works unchanged. (Without a proxy, the API would need **CORS** (*Cross-Origin Resource Sharing*) rules saying which other origins may call it.)

### fetch doesn't fail on 400

`fetch` only rejects when there's no answer at all: the server is down, or the network is. A 400 or a 500 is still an answer, so the promise resolves, and `response.ok` (true for 200–299) is how you tell:

```jsx
const response = await fetch(url);
const data = await response.json();
if (!response.ok) {
  // data is problem details, not your rows
}
```

ASP.NET Core sends errors as **problem details**: JSON with a `title`, a `status` and sometimes more. `Results.Problem(title: "…", statusCode: 400)` makes one. Show the `title`; don't try to `map` over it.

### Effects and their dependencies

`useEffect(fn, deps)` runs `fn` after a render whenever something in `deps` changed:

| deps | runs |
|---|---|
| `[]` | once, after the first render |
| `[division]` | first render, then whenever `division` changes |
| left out | after **every** render |

Leave the array out of an effect that fetches and sets state, and you get a loop: every answer causes a render, every render fetches again. The **Network** tab shows it as a wall of identical requests.

### The Network tab

The **Network** tab is Codegrove's version of the browser's developer tools: method, path, status, time, the body you sent and the one that came back, and anything the endpoint printed. When the page looks wrong, find out which side is wrong first: did the right request go out, and did the right answer come back?

### New words

- **Frontend / backend**: the program in the browser, and the program on the server that owns the data.
- **Origin**: a scheme, host and port, like `http://localhost:5173`. Requests to the same origin need no extra permission.
- **Proxy**: a server in the middle that forwards requests, like Vite sending `/api` on to the API.
- **CORS** (*Cross-Origin Resource Sharing*): rules a server sends to say which other origins may call it.
- **Problem details**: ASP.NET Core's standard JSON for errors, with a `title` and a `status`.
- **Dependency array**: the second argument of `useEffect`; the effect runs again when one of its values changes.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A dice roller with its own API. `GET /api/roll?sides=6` answers a roll; anything outside 2 to 100 gets **400** with problem details. Click **d20**, then **d1000**, and watch the **Network** tab: the effect runs again whenever `sides` changes, and the page shows the problem's `title`. Try removing `[sides]` from the effect and press **▶ Run** to see what a missing dependency array does.

lessons.title: Start a new club
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Sending things to your server

Your Club Hub can **show** clubs. Now kids in the Grove want to **start** clubs too! The server has a new job ready for that: `POST /api/clubs`. Your page needs a form that sends it a new club.

You'll build on **your own code** from the last milestone: your `App.jsx` comes along.

### GET asks, POST sends

So far, every `fetch` was a **GET**: "please give me something". A **POST** says "here's something new, please keep it". You tell `fetch` three extra things:

```jsx
await fetch("/api/clubs", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: "Snail Racers", meets: "Thursday" }),
});
```

- `method`: what kind of request it is.
- `headers`: a note that says "the body is JSON".
- `body`: the new club, turned into JSON text with `JSON.stringify`.

### When the server says no

A club with no name? The server answers **400 Bad Request** and a message: `"A club needs a name."`. `fetch` still gives you the answer, so check `response.ok`. It's `true` when everything worked. If it's `false`, show the server's message.

### Load the list again

After a new club is added, the page should show it. Put your `fetch` from last time in a function called `loadClubs`. Then `useEffect` can call it when the page opens, and the form can call it after adding a club.

### New words

- **POST**: a request that sends something new for the server to keep.
- **Request body**: the data you send with a request, like the new club.
- **Status code**: the number the server answers with, like 200 (OK) or 400 (Bad Request).
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A guestbook with its own server. Type your name and press **Sign**: the page sends `POST /api/guests`, then loads the list again. Press **Sign** with an empty box to see the server say no. Watch it all happen in the **Network** tab.

lessons.title: API: record results
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Writing data safely

Reading data is the easy half. As soon as an API accepts writes, it has to decide what a client may change, and what to say when a request is wrong. A good API answers bad input with a clear, structured error, so the frontend can show it next to the right field. In this milestone the Junior League's API learns to record match results, and your standings page from last time comes along to show them.

### Bind a DTO, not an entity

A **DTO** (*Data Transfer Object*) is a small type shaped like the request, not like the table:

```csharp
public record NewMatch(
    int HomeTeamId, int AwayTeamId,
    int HomeGoals, int AwayGoals);
```

Bind the entity (`Match`) instead, and the client controls every property, `Id` included. That's **overposting**. Here, a client that sends `"id": 1` makes EF Core try to add a second match with key 1, and the request ends in a 500. With a DTO, the server copies only the fields it accepts and picks the id itself.

### Validation problem details

Check the input before touching the database, collect every problem, and answer them all at once:

```csharp
var errors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>();
if (input.HomeGoals < 0)
    errors["homeGoals"] = ["Goals can't be below 0."];
if (errors.Count > 0)
    return Results.ValidationProblem(errors);
```

That's a **400** with problem details plus an `errors` object keyed by field. Next milestone, your form shows each message next to its field. (Controllers with `[ApiController]` did this from DataAnnotations automatically. Minimal APIs leave it to you.)

### Status codes for writes

| Request | Worked | Didn't |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/matches` | **201 Created**, a `Location` header and the new match | **400** with the errors |
| `GET /api/matches/7` | **200 OK** | **404 Not Found** |
| `DELETE /api/matches/7` | **204 No Content** | **404 Not Found** |

### Trying an API without a frontend

Your page doesn't have a results form yet. Open the **Network** tab and use **Send a request**: it sends any method, path and JSON body to your running API, and logs the answer like the page's own requests. (In a real project that's a `.http` file, Swagger UI or Postman.) Record a result, then click a division on your page to see the standings move.

### New words

- **DTO** (*Data Transfer Object*): a type shaped like one request or response, kept apart from the database entities.
- **Overposting**: a client setting properties it shouldn't, because the API bound a whole entity.
- **Validation problem details**: a 400 with problem details and an `errors` object of messages per field.
- **Location header**: where a 201 says the new resource can be found, like `/api/matches/7`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A notes API: `POST /api/notes` takes a `NewNote` (text only), answers **201** with a `Location`, or a validation problem when the text is empty; `DELETE` answers **204** or **404**. Open the **Network** tab, choose **Send a request**, and POST `{ "text": "Hello" }` to `/api/notes`. Then press **Refresh** on the page. Try an empty text, and a DELETE of a note that isn't there.
